title: Andrew Kelley Interview: Why He Built Zig, Banned AI Contributions, and Moved Zig off GitHub
gist: Zig creator Andrew Kelley explains why the project categorically bans AI-generated contributions (they are low-quality, waste finite maintainer review time, and produce contributors who never grow into core team members) and why Zig migrated its repository from GitHub to the nonprofit Codeberg after persistent CI failures, a decision he links to misaligned incentives at GitHub as AI workloads surge.

themes.theme: The case against AI contributions in open source

insights.claim: Andrew Kelley says AI-generated code contributions to Zig are invariably low quality and have negative value because they consume maintainer review time; after a few review rounds it becomes clear the AI-driven contributor doesn't understand the code, is pasting reviewer feedback back into a chatbot and laundering the response to hide that they're using AI, and the contribution never reaches acceptable quality.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: A specific, named failure mode ('laundering the chat') that maintainers of other open-source projects can watch for; supports a broader thesis that AI-assisted PRs impose a net-negative time tax on scarce maintainer attention in projects with rigorous review standards.
insights.quote: Not only that, they have negative value […] When we get these slop contributions, they take our review time and then after a few reviews, we realize they have no clue what they're doing. They're just pasting what we say back to the chat and then laundering the chat back to pretend that they're not using chat, but we can still tell.
insights.locator: The first reason is just that those kinds of contributions

insights.claim: Kelley frames code review as a mentorship investment of the project's limited time, deliberately betting on contributors likely to grow into long-term core team members ('contributor poker') over drive-by contributors, and states that people using AI always fall into the drive-by category because they aren't learning anything and won't join the core team later.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: A generalizable open-source governance framework ('contributor poker') that other maintainers facing AI-contribution floods could adopt: treat review time as a scarce investment allocated toward human contributor development, not toward processing volume.
insights.quote: The idea of contributor poker is that we have limited time. So we want to notice: okay, who can we invest our time in to help them become better programmers, better contributors for the project? And who is maybe a drive-by contributor? And so people who are using AI, they're always in the second category.
insights.locator: Equally importantly, Kelley stressed Zig's core educational mission

insights.claim: Zig's principled anti-AI-contribution stance contrasts directly with Bun, which recently rewrote its entire codebase from Zig to Rust using numerous AI agents to port, verify, and fix code; Kelley wrote a critical response titled 'My Thoughts on the Bun Rust Rewrite' arguing the disagreement was not about Zig vs. Rust language features but about the diverging value systems of the two projects.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: Illustrates a real fork in industry philosophy on AI-assisted engineering between two adjacent systems-language projects — a useful case study contrast for evaluating how differently companies/projects are adopting agentic coding at scale.
insights.quote: The main issue here had nothing to do with the language features of Zig vs Rust, and everything to do with the diverging value systems of the two projects.
insights.locator: Zig's principled approach contrasts with the approach of Bun

insights.claim: Zig moved its repository from GitHub to the German nonprofit Codeberg because GitHub Actions CI runs had been persistently and unpredictably failing to produce results; after the move, Zig's CI worked again.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: A concrete, verifiable operational complaint against GitHub's CI reliability from a high-profile open-source project — worth watching for whether other projects cite similar GitHub Actions degradation.
insights.quote: GitHub simply stopped working for us. We would not have results for our continuous integration runs anymore. It just would stop working. So we moved to Codeberg and now our continuous integration server works again
insights.locator: Kelley further explains that the project moved its GitHub repository

insights.claim: Kelley says he finds nonprofits like Codeberg to be a more stable business model than startups or corporations because nonprofits aren't chasing the next quarter's profitability, whereas corporations are, and that stability is what he wants for Zig's infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: An explicit incentive-alignment argument for open-source infrastructure choices favoring nonprofit hosts over VC-backed/corporate platforms — relevant to how open-source foundations and maintainers may evaluate platform dependency risk going forward.
insights.quote: Codeberg is also a German nonprofit and personally I find using nonprofits to be a more stable business than startups or corporations, because these corporations are always chasing the next thing and trying to make the next quarter more profitable. Nonprofits are just trying to keep doing what they're doing, and that stability is what I want.
insights.locator: Kelley also emphasized a better alignment of incentives

insights.claim: Some developers responding to the news agreed that GitHub's performance decline coincided with an exponential increase in AI workloads on the platform.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: An unverified but notable community-sourced hypothesis linking GitHub's infrastructure strain to surging AI-agent traffic (e.g., automated PR/CI load) — worth monitoring as a potential systemic risk for GitHub-dependent CI pipelines.
insights.locator: Some developers concurred with the perceived decrease

insights.claim: Kelley conceived Zig while trying to build a native digital audio workstation: JavaScript lacked low-level hardware control, Go's stop-the-world garbage collection pauses compromised real-time audio playback, Rust (pre-1.0) imposed borrow-checker friction that derailed UI font rendering for weeks, and C++ produced persistent memory corruption bugs that consumed extensive debugging time.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: Explains Zig's design motivation as a reaction to specific, named limitations in four competing languages for real-time/systems programming — useful context for why Zig has found a niche in low-latency and embedded domains.
insights.locator: Kelley recalled in the interview conceiving Zig

insights.claim: The Zig language rejects automatic memory management in favor of explicit memory allocators; Andrew Kelley quit his job in 2018 to build Zig full-time.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: Core design choice (explicit allocators, no GC) that differentiates Zig from Go and positions it closer to C/Rust for systems programming use cases.
insights.locator: The Zig language rejects automatic memory management

insights.claim: Zig powers Ghostty (a terminal emulator), TigerBeetle (a low-latency financial database), and Uber's cross-compilation infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Bruno Couriol
insights.so_what: Concrete production adoption signal for Zig beyond hobbyist use, including a financial-infrastructure use case (TigerBeetle) and a major tech company's build tooling (Uber) — evidence of real enterprise traction.
insights.locator: Zig powers Ghostty, the low-latency financial database TigerBeetle
